title: Architecture Content Framework — Deliverables and Artifacts by Phase

blocks.text: SESSION 1 — Concept · Key Points · Memory Technique. Read, absorb, stop.
1. Concept Explained Simply

The Architecture Content Framework answers: "For any given ADM phase, what specific catalogs, matrices, and diagrams should I produce — and why?" Recall the three artifact types from Lesson 4: Catalogs (lists of things), Matrices (relationships between things), Diagrams (pictures of things). The Content Framework applies this systematically to every ADM phase — a tested, standard menu of outputs proven to answer the questions stakeholders actually ask.
2. Key Points
Four content concepts — **BCMD**:

rows: An entity of a particular type within the metamodel (e.g., a business service "Purchase Order"). Carries metadata supporting query and analysis.
A list of building blocks of a specific type, used for governance or reference (e.g., an organisation chart)
A grid showing relationships between two or more model entities — used when relationships are list-based, not graphical (e.g., a CRUD matrix)
A graphical rendering of architectural content for visual stakeholder communication

blocks.text: Key artifacts by phase:

rows: Value Chain, Solution Concept, Business Model, Business Capability Map, Value Stream Map
Organization/Actor, Driver/Goal/Objective, Role, Business Service/Function, Location, Process/Event/Control/Product, Contract/Measure
Business Footprint, Functional Decomposition, Process Flow, Use-Case
Conceptual Data, Logical Data, Data Security, Data Migration, Data Dissemination
Application Communication, Application Migration, Software Distribution
Environments and Locations, Platform Decomposition, Networked Computing

blocks.text: **Data Entity/Business Function Matrix vs Application/Data Matrix**: The former shows which business functions create/read/update/delete which data entities (CRUD, governance/ownership). The latter shows which applications use which data entities (dependency/migration scope). Different purposes — frequently confused.
**Content Framework and the ADM**: The ADM tells you when to produce artifacts; the Content Framework tells you what those artifacts should specifically be and what metamodel entities each contains.
3. Memory Technique

BCMD: Building Block → Catalog → Matrix → Diagram.

Artifact-type pattern by phase stage: Early phases (Preliminary, A) = mostly diagrams + one catalog (broad orientation). Middle phases (B, C, D) = heaviest catalogs and matrices (detailed governance). Late phases (E, F) = return to diagrams (programme-level communication).

EXAM TRAP 1 — NOT EQUAL ARTIFACT VOLUME ACROSS PHASES. Phases B and C produce the largest number of catalogs and matrices — governance traceability is highest there. Phase A and E are lighter, mostly diagrams.

EXAM TRAP 2 — DATA ENTITY/BUSINESS FUNCTION MATRIX ≠ APPLICATION/DATA MATRIX. One is about business process governance (CRUD by function); the other is about application/data dependency mapping. Frequently confused on the exam.

EXAM TRAP 3 — CATALOG ≠ MATRIX EVEN WHEN BOTH ARE TABLES. A catalog lists one type of thing. A matrix cross-references two or more dimensions. One column of entities = catalog. Cross-referenced dimensions = matrix.

EXAM TRAP 4 — CONTENT FRAMEWORK ≠ ENTERPRISE CONTINUUM ≠ ARCHITECTURE REPOSITORY. Three distinct concepts. Content Framework = what to produce. Enterprise Continuum = classification by genericity. Architecture Repository = storage. Easily confused if not clearly separated.
✋ PAUSE POINT — CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING. Answer from memory before reading Session 2.
1. Name the four content concepts (BCMD) with a one-sentence definition each.

Building Block — an entity within the metamodel. Catalog — a list of building blocks of one type. Matrix — a grid of relationships between two or more entity types. Diagram — a graphical rendering for visual communication.
2. What is the difference between the Data Entity/Business Function Matrix and the Application/Data Matrix?

Data Entity/Business Function Matrix = which business functions CRUD which data entities (ownership/governance). Application/Data Matrix = which applications use which data entities (migration scope/dependency).
3. Which phases produce the heaviest concentration of catalogs and matrices, and why?

Phase B and Phase C (Data and Application) — these require the most detailed governance traceability. Early (Preliminary, A) and late (E, F) phases rely more on diagrams for broad orientation and communication.
SESSION 2 — Real-World Example · How It Works in Practice · Practice Questions · Part 2 Scenario
4. Real-World Example — GlobalTech Dynamics 365

items: **Preliminary**: Principles Catalog — the six Architecture Principles, each in NSRI format.

**Phase A**: Stakeholder Catalog (CFO, Head of Finance, IT Ops, DPO, invisible team). Solution Concept Diagram (SAP → Dynamics 365 sketch). Business Capability Map (Finance and HR capabilities at a glance).
**Phase B**: Business Service/Function Catalog (GL, AP, AR, Fixed Assets, Financial Reporting as formal functions). Contract/Measure Catalog (the "3-day close" SLA as a trackable measure).

**Phase C (Data)**: Data Entity/Data Component Catalog (all 14 master data entities including the new Absence Record). Data Entity/Business Function Matrix — would have surfaced the SAP-to-AD identity reconciliation gap earlier had it existed at Baseline time. Data Security Diagram (personal data flows, reviewed by DPO).

**Phase C (Application)**: Application Portfolio Catalog (SAP ECC, SAP HR, Procurement, Power BI, AD → target: Dynamics 365 Finance/HR, API Management, Data Factory). Application Interaction Matrix — the artifact underlying the Procurement→Finance and Audit→Finance integration mapping.
**Phase D**: Technology Standards Catalog (Azure services, TLS 1.3, SAML 2.0). Platform Decomposition Diagram (App Service + SQL + AD + API Management = the Dynamics 365 stack).
**Phase E**: Benefits Diagram — connects WP3 (Finance Core) to its $280k/year savings.

blocks.text: 5. How It Actually Works in Practice

REALITY CHECK: NOBODY PRODUCES EVERY ARTIFACT. EA teams select the subset that matters, driven by stakeholder concerns (Lesson 9) and transformation scale. A small Segment programme might produce five or six artifacts; GlobalTech's enterprise-wide, regulated programme produces a dozen or more.

REALITY CHECK: MATRICES ARE THE MOST COMMONLY SKIPPED — AND MOST COSTLY TO SKIP. Diagrams are visually satisfying; catalogs feel like straightforward inventory. Matrices — systematically mapping every entity of one type against another — are tedious and often skipped under time pressure. But the Application/Data Matrix is exactly what would have surfaced the Power BI-to-SAP dependency before it became an urgent discovery.
6. Part 1 Practice Questions
Q1. Which correctly describes a "Matrix" as a content concept?

items: A) A list of building blocks of a specific type, used for governance
B) A grid showing relationships between two or more model entities, used when relationships are difficult to show graphically ✓
C) A graphical rendering of architectural content for visual retrieval
D) An entity within the metamodel carrying metadata for query and analysis

blocks.text: Answer: B — precise definition. A = Catalog; C = Diagram; D = Building Block.
Q2. An architect needs to know which applications create, read, update, or delete customer data, to plan a migration. Which artifact?

items: A) The Data Entity/Data Component Catalog

blocks.text: Answer: B — shows which applications use which data entities, exactly what's needed for migration scoping.
Q3. Which best describes the relationship between the Content Framework and the Enterprise Continuum?

items: A) The same concept — both classify artifacts from generic to organisation-specific
B) Content Framework defines what to produce at each phase; Enterprise Continuum classifies assets from generic to organisation-specific — distinct concepts ✓
C) Content Framework is a subset of the Enterprise Continuum
D) Enterprise Continuum defines artifacts; Content Framework stores them

blocks.text: Answer: B — two distinct concepts. Confusing them is a common exam error.
7. Part 2 Scenario Question (Exam-Authentic Format)

SCENARIO: Phase C is complete. The EA team produced an Application Portfolio Catalog, Interface Catalog, and several diagrams — but no Application Interaction Matrix or Application/Data Matrix. The Head of IT Operations says: "We have the diagrams — they show the same information visually. Do we really need the matrices too?"

rows: Agree — the diagram makes the matrix redundant. Misunderstands the different purposes: a diagram cannot support systematic queries like "which of our 40 applications depend on the Customer entity?"
Disagree — every catalog/matrix/diagram in the Content Framework must be produced without exception. Overly rigid; the Standard allows tailoring based on programme needs.

Disagree with "duplicate work" — diagrams communicate visually to a broad audience; matrices support systematic governance queries impractical from a diagram alone. Tie the decision to GlobalTech's actual need: SAP decommissioning requires the Application/Data Matrix for migration scoping — not optional given the governance decisions Phase C must inform. Best answer.
Escalate to the Architecture Board as a Compliance breach. Disproportionate — a content gap is addressed through normal EA practice, not Board escalation.
